title: Pomegranate: fiber, sugar and nutrients

seo.title: Pomegranate: fiber, sugar and nutrients
seo.meta_description: Pomegranate arils provide about 83 calories, 4 g fiber and 13.7 g sugar per 100 g, plus potassium, vitamin C and polyphenols. Whole arils differ from juice.
seo.search_intent: Understand pomegranate nutrition, fiber, sugar and its main polyphenols

excerpt: Pomegranate arils provide about 83 calories, 4 g fiber and 13.7 g naturally occurring sugar per 100 g, along with about 236 mg potassium, 10 mg vitamin C and 38 mcg folate. Their polyphenols include anthocyanins and ellagitannins, while juice generally loses much of the fiber found in whole arils.
content_html:
Pomegranate is often introduced through the word antioxidants, but its nutrition story starts with something more ordinary and useful: whole pomegranate arils are a fiber-containing fruit.

What 100 g of arils provides

NutrientPer 100 g
Calories83
Fiber4.0 g
Sugars13.7 g
Protein1.7 g
Potassium236 mg
Vitamin C10.2 mg
Folate38 mcg

A half-cup portion around 87 g works out to roughly 72 calories, 3.5 g fiber and 12 g sugar.

The sugar is natural, but it still counts

Pomegranate contains more sugar per 100 g than strawberries and somewhat more than blueberries in standard USDA references. That does not make it ‘too sugary.’ The sugars are eaten inside a whole-fruit matrix that also contains water and fiber.

Juicing changes that matrix. Juice keeps sugars and many soluble compounds but removes much of the fibrous structure and is easier to consume quickly.

Which polyphenols are present?

The red-purple color comes partly from anthocyanins. Pomegranate also contains ellagitannins, including punicalagins, especially abundant in peel and membranes and present to varying degrees in juices depending on processing.

Ellagic-acid-related compounds can be transformed by gut microbes into urolithins. People differ in how efficiently they produce those metabolites.

More polyphenols does not turn fruit into medicine

Pomegranate extracts have been studied in many clinical settings, but results from concentrated extracts cannot automatically be assigned to a half cup of arils. Dose, formulation and duration are different.

Arils or juice?

If fiber and chewing matter, whole arils have the clear advantage. Juice can still fit into a diet, but it generally provides little or no fiber depending on processing.

Pomegranate makes more sense nutritionally as a whole fruit than as a container for one antioxidant number.

Whole arils, juice, and extracts are not equivalent

Eating the arils means eating the juicy seed sacs together with their edible seed material, which is where the fiber in the USDA profile comes from. A bowl of arils therefore behaves like whole fruit: it takes time to chew, has substantial volume, and supplies fiber along with its naturally occurring sugars. Pomegranate juice is easier to drink quickly and contains little of that intact fiber, so the same fruit can have a different nutritional effect depending on the form.

Commercial juice also varies in concentration and ingredients. Some bottles are 100 percent pomegranate juice; others are blends with grape, apple, or other juices, and sweetened beverages may contain added sugar. The front label can emphasize pomegranate even when it is not the only juice present. Checking the ingredient list and serving size is the fastest way to distinguish a concentrated pomegranate product from a flavored juice drink.

Polyphenol numbers deserve similar context. Punicalagins, ellagic-acid-related compounds, anthocyanins, and other phenolics can differ by cultivar, processing, storage, and which parts of the fruit are included. A juice pressed with more contact from peel or membranes may not match a hand-eaten bowl of arils. Laboratory antioxidant measurements are useful for describing composition, but they are not a direct measure of what a serving will do in a person's body.

The seeds inside the arils are edible and contribute to texture. Some people enjoy the crunch; others prefer juice because they dislike it. If fiber is one of your reasons for choosing pomegranate, swallowing the whole aril is the more relevant form. Sprinkling arils on yogurt, oatmeal, salads, roasted vegetables, or grain dishes can add a moderate portion without requiring you to eat an entire fruit at once.

Pomegranate is therefore best understood as a nutrient-dense fruit rather than a medicinal shortcut. Its fiber, potassium, vitamin C, folate, and diverse polyphenols are worthwhile, but the usual principles still apply: portion, overall diet, and food form matter. A half-cup of arils can be an easy serving; a large bottle of juice is a much more concentrated way to consume the fruit's sugars.

Opening a pomegranate is easier if you score the rind, pull the fruit into sections, and loosen the arils over a bowl rather than cutting straight through everything. That reduces juice loss and makes the edible portion easier to portion. Prepared cups of arils cost more but can be worthwhile when convenience determines whether the fruit gets eaten at all.

faq.question: How much fiber is in pomegranate?
faq.answer: About 4 g per 100 g of arils, or roughly 3.5 g in a half-cup portion around 87 g.

faq.question: How much sugar is in pomegranate?
faq.answer: About 13.7 g per 100 g of arils, naturally occurring in the fruit.

faq.question: Which polyphenols are important in pomegranate?
faq.answer: Anthocyanins and ellagitannins, including punicalagins, are among the best-known compounds.

faq.question: Is pomegranate juice the same as eating the arils?
faq.answer: No. Juice keeps sugars and soluble compounds but loses much of the fiber and structure of the whole fruit.
